15440: Succulent means full of juice, richness, and satisfying goodness. It is always a positive word — it never describes something bad or unpleasant. When you call something succulent, you are saying it is not just good, but pleasurably, almost irresistibly good.

This is the most common way the word is used.

When food is succulent, it means it is:

  • Juicy — full of natural moisture and liquid
  • Tender — soft and easy to bite into
  • Flavorful — rich in taste, not bland or dry

Think about biting into a perfectly cooked piece of chicken. The juice runs out, the meat is soft, and the flavor is deep and satisfying. That is succulent food.

Now imagine the opposite — dry, tough, flavorless chicken. That is the complete opposite of succulent.

Examples:

  • "The chef prepared a succulent lamb roast."
  • "She bit into a succulent, ripe mango."
  • "The prawns were succulent and perfectly seasoned."

What makes "succulent" special compared to just saying "juicy"?
"Juicy" simply means liquid is present. "Succulent" goes further — it suggests that the food is richly satisfying as a whole, combining juiciness, tenderness, and good flavor together. It is a fuller, more indulgent compliment. A menu using the word "succulent" is trying to make your mouth water.

The word has a well-established second meaning in the world of plants.

A succulent plant is one that has thick, fleshy, swollen leaves or stems that store water inside them. This adaptation allows the plant to survive in hot, dry environments like deserts, where rainfall is rare.

The logic connects directly to Meaning 1 — just as succulent food is full of moisture and richness, a succulent plant is literally full of stored water, making its parts thick and almost "juicy-looking."

Famous examples of succulent plants:

  • Aloe vera — the gel-filled plant used in skincare
  • Cactus — spiky desert plants with water-storing stems
  • Jade plant — a popular houseplant with thick, glossy leaves
  • Echeveria — a rosette-shaped plant commonly kept indoors

Succulent plants are extremely popular as houseplants because they require very little watering and are hard to kill.

Examples of the word used this way:

  • "Her windowsill was lined with small succulents." (Here, "succulents" is used as a noun, but the root meaning is the same adjective.)
  • "The garden featured a beautiful display of succulent plants."
Meaning 3: Describing Something Richly Appealing (Figurative Use)

Less commonly, writers and speakers use "succulent" in a figurative way to describe something that is richly attractive, tempting, or deeply interesting — not food or plants, but ideas, opportunities, or details.

Examples:

  • "The journalist uncovered some succulent details about the scandal." (Meaning: rich, juicy, fascinating details)
  • "It was a succulent business opportunity — too good to pass up." (Meaning: rich, highly attractive)

This figurative use borrows the sense of "richly satisfying goodness" from the food meaning and applies it to non-physical things. You will encounter this mostly in writing, not everyday conversation.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Succulent" is a sensory word — it paints a vivid picture and almost makes you feel something. It's slightly more formal and expressive than plain words like "juicy" or "moist." You'll often see it in:

  • Restaurant menus and food writing
  • Recipe descriptions
  • Gardening and nature writing
  • Literary or journalistic prose

It is never a negative word. You would never use it to describe something bad. If someone calls your cooking "succulent," take it as a high compliment.

ContextWhat "succulent" means
FoodJuicy, tender, rich, and deeply flavorful
PlantsHaving thick, fleshy parts that store water
FigurativeRichly attractive, tempting, or fascinatingly detailed

In one sentence: Succulent describes something that is richly full of moisture, flavor, or goodness — whether it's a piece of meat, a desert plant, or even an irresistible opportunity.
15441:
Imagine you are in a tug-of-war. You are pulling as hard as you can, trying not to lose. But the force on the other side is stronger than you. Slowly, your grip weakens. Your feet start sliding. And finally — you let go. You couldn't hold on anymore.

That moment of giving in — that is succumbing.

"Succumb" means to stop resisting something that is stronger than you, and give in to it — usually because you have no choice, or because the force is simply too powerful to fight off any longer.

The word almost always implies that a struggle happened first. The person or thing was holding on, resisting, fighting — and then couldn't anymore.

1. To give in to a force, pressure, temptation, or influence

This is the most common use. Someone is trying to resist something — and eventually, that something wins.

Examples:

  • She had been on a strict diet for months, but she finally succumbed to the temptation of chocolate cake.
  • He knew smoking was harmful, but he succumbed to peer pressure and started anyway.
  • The negotiators held firm for weeks, but eventually succumbed to the other side's demands.
  • Despite his fear, he almost succumbed to the urge to run away.

In all these examples, notice the pattern: there was a fight, and the fight was lost.

2. To die as a result of an illness or injury

This is a more formal and serious use. It means someone was fighting a disease or the effects of an injury, but could not survive it.

Examples:

  • He succumbed to cancer after a three-year battle.
  • The patient succumbed to his injuries at the hospital.
  • Thousands of people succumbed to the disease during the epidemic.

This usage is common in news writing, medical contexts, and formal speech. You would not use this meaning lightly or casually.

A few things make this word more precise and powerful than simpler alternatives:

It always implies prior resistance. This is the most important thing to remember. If someone happily and willingly accepts something with no struggle, you would not use "succumb." The word carries the weight of a fight that was eventually lost. Compare:

  • "She accepted the job offer." → No struggle. She just said yes.
  • "She finally succumbed to her boss's repeated requests to take the promotion." → She resisted for a while, but eventually gave in.

It almost always implies the outcome was unwanted. The person did not want to give in. They were trying not to. This makes the word carry a slightly sad or unfortunate tone.

It can apply to both physical and non-physical forces:

  • Physical: illness, injury, exhaustion, fire, a storm
  • Non-physical: temptation, fear, desire, pressure, curiosity, grief, charm

Understanding what a word is not is just as important as understanding what it is.

It is not the same as simply "failing."
Failing means you tried to do something and did not succeed. Succumbing means something overwhelmed you and overcame your resistance. The focus is different.

  • "He failed the exam." → He didn't pass.
  • "He succumbed to anxiety before the exam." → Anxiety overcame him.

It is not exactly the same as "surrendering."
Surrendering is usually a conscious, deliberate decision — a formal act of giving up. Succumbing can be more passive — something just overcomes you. You may not even fully realize it's happening.

It is not the same as "agreeing."
If you agree with someone after hearing their argument, you simply changed your mind. If you succumb to someone's pressure, you gave in despite not really wanting to — the pressure wore you down.
The Grammar Rule: Always Followed by "to"

This is important. "Succumb" is almost always followed by the word "to." You always succumb to something — to a disease, to temptation, to pressure, to fear.

  • ✅ She succumbed to exhaustion.
  • ✅ He succumbed to the illness.
  • ❌ She succumbed exhaustion. (incorrect)

"Succumb" is a formal or semi-formal word. You will see it often in news articles, literature, medical writing, and serious speech. In casual everyday conversation, people might instead say "gave in," "caved," or "couldn't resist" — these mean similar things but sound more informal. "Succumb" is the more precise, more dignified version.

To succumb = to stop resisting something stronger than you and give in to it — whether that is a temptation, a pressure, an emotion, or a fatal illness — often reluctantly, and after a period of struggle.
15442:
When something is described as sudorific, it means it causes sweating or promotes perspiration. That's the whole idea in a nutshell. If a thing — a medicine, a food, a plant, a treatment — has the ability to make your body produce sweat, that thing is sudorific.

Think of it this way: your body sweats for a reason. Sweating cools you down, releases certain waste products, and is one of the ways your body tries to fight illness. Anything that deliberately triggers or noticeably increases this sweating response is called sudorific.
What kinds of things can be sudorific?

The adjective "sudorific" is used to describe a wide range of things:

Medicines and drugs — Certain medications, especially older or traditional ones, are sudorific. Doctors or herbalists might prescribe them specifically to make a feverish patient sweat, because sweating helps break a fever and cool the body down.

Herbs and plants — Many plants have sudorific properties. Elderflower, yarrow, ginger, and boneset are classic examples used in herbal medicine for centuries. If you've ever had ginger tea when you were sick and noticed you started sweating, that's a sudorific effect in action.

Foods and spices — Spicy foods like chili peppers or cayenne are sudorific. When you eat something very spicy and your forehead starts to bead with sweat, that's because capsaicin (the compound that makes chilies hot) has a sudorific effect on the body.

Treatments and environments — A steam bath, a sauna, or a hot compress can also be described as sudorific because they cause the body to sweat significantly.

"Sudorific" is a formal, medical, and pharmacological term. You won't hear it much in everyday conversation — no one walks into a room on a hot day and says, "Wow, it's quite sudorific in here!" Instead, you're more likely to encounter it in:

  • Medical textbooks or pharmacology guides
  • Herbal medicine and naturopathy literature
  • Historical medical writing (it was very commonly used in older medical texts)
  • Academic or scientific articles about sweat glands, fever management, or plant-based medicine
How to use it in a sentence

Here are a few natural examples that show how the adjective works:

  • "The physician recommended a sudorific herb to help the patient sweat through the fever."
  • "Ginger is well known for its sudorific properties in traditional medicine."
  • "The sudorific effect of the hot steam room left everyone dripping."
  • "Doctors once relied heavily on sudorific treatments before modern fever-reducing drugs existed."
  • "The spicy soup had a surprisingly sudorific effect on everyone at the table."

Being sudorific is usually understood as a functional property — a quality that something has and exerts on the body. So when you call something sudorific, you're making a statement about its effect or capability, not just its temperature or intensity.

For example, a hot day might make you sweat, but we don't typically call a hot day "sudorific" in a medical sense — the word is more precisely reserved for things that actively trigger the sweat response through a physiological mechanism, like a drug stimulating the sweat glands, or a herb activating the body's heat-release system.

To summarize everything: sudorific is an adjective that means sweat-inducing. It's used to describe any substance, treatment, food, or agent that causes or promotes sweating in the body. The word belongs mostly to the world of medicine, pharmacology, and herbal science, where causing controlled sweating is sometimes a desired and therapeutic outcome — particularly for breaking fevers or cleansing the body. If you remember just one thing, remember this: sudorific = sweat-causing.
15443: To sue someone means to take them to a court of law and formally demand that they compensate you or fix a wrong they have done to you. It is a legal action that one person or organization initiates against another. When you sue someone, you are essentially saying to a court: "This person/company has wronged me, and I want the law to make it right."

Imagine your neighbor's dog bites you badly, and you end up with expensive hospital bills. Your neighbor refuses to help. You can sue them — meaning you go to court, present your case, and ask a judge to legally force your neighbor to pay for your medical expenses. The court then decides who is right.

That's suing in its most straightforward form.

When someone sues and someone gets sued, there are two sides:

  • The person doing the suing is called the plaintiff — the one who feels wronged and starts the case.
  • The person being sued is called the defendant — the one who has to go to court and defend themselves.

You can sue a person, a company, an organization, or even a government.

People sue for many reasons, all centered around the idea that someone caused them harm or violated their rights. Common reasons include:

  • Someone injured you physically (a car accident, a dog bite, a slip and fall on someone's unsafe property)
  • Someone broke a promise that was written in a contract (didn't deliver goods, didn't pay for services)
  • Someone damaged your reputation by spreading lies about you (this is called defamation)
  • A doctor made a serious mistake during your treatment (medical malpractice)
  • A company sold you a defective product that harmed you
  • An employer treated you unfairly based on your race, gender, religion, etc. (discrimination)
  • Someone damaged or stole your property
What Can You Get From Suing?

When you sue someone, you are typically asking for one or both of the following:

1. Money (called "damages")
This is the most common outcome. The court orders the other party to pay you a sum of money to compensate for your loss, suffering, or expenses. For example, if someone crashed into your car, you might sue for the repair costs plus any medical bills.

2. A Court Order (called an "injunction")
Sometimes you don't just want money — you want someone to stop doing something or start doing something. For example, if a factory near your home is illegally polluting the river, you might sue to get a court order that forces them to stop. The court can legally compel a behavior, not just award money.
Suing Is a Civil Matter, Not Criminal

This is an important distinction that confuses many people.

Criminal cases are brought by the government (the state or the country) against a person who broke the law. The punishment is usually a fine, imprisonment, or both. Ordinary citizens don't "sue" in criminal cases — the government prosecutes.

Civil cases — which is where "suing" happens — are brought by a private person or organization against another private person or organization. The goal is not to put someone in jail, but to get compensation or enforce rights.

So, if someone steals from you:

  • The government might prosecute them criminally (which could lead to jail time).
  • You might sue them civilly (to get your money or property back).

Both can happen at the same time, and they are entirely separate processes.

When you sue someone, you file a formal document with the court explaining your complaint. The other side is informed and gets a chance to respond. Both sides then present their evidence and arguments, and eventually a judge (or sometimes a jury) decides the outcome. If you win, the court issues a ruling in your favor. If you lose, you get nothing — and may even have to pay the other side's legal costs in some cases.

Many lawsuits never reach a full trial. The two sides often reach a settlement — a private agreement (usually involving a payment) — before a judge makes a final ruling. You will often hear phrases like "they settled out of court," which means they resolved it without a judge's final decision.

The word is very flexible:

  • She decided to sue the company for wrongful termination.
  • He was sued by his former business partner.
  • They threatened to sue if the refund wasn't issued.
  • The family sued the hospital for negligence.
  • You can sue for damages even if the amount is small — small claims court exists for that.
  • The construction company was sued over the building collapse.

Note the common pattern: sue + someone + for + reason/amount.
"She sued the driver for $50,000 in damages."

In older, formal, or literary English, "sue" can also mean to make a humble or earnest appeal — to plead or petition for something. This usage is rare today, but you may encounter it in older books or historical texts.

Examples:

  • The defeated army sued for peace. (They formally appealed for peace.)
  • He sued for mercy before the king. (He pleaded for mercy.)

This meaning shares the same spirit as the legal meaning — making a formal request — but it is not used in everyday modern speech. If you encounter it, it simply means "to earnestly appeal or petition."

To sue is to formally use the legal system to seek justice or compensation from someone who has wronged you. It is a civil (not criminal) action. The person suing wants either money, a court-enforced action, or both. A judge or jury ultimately decides the outcome, though most cases end in a settlement before that point.
15444: Suede is a type of soft, velvety leather with a fuzzy surface. It is used to make shoes, jackets, bags, and many other products.
What suede actually is

An animal's skin has two sides: the outer side (the part that faced the world, exposed to sun and air) and the inner side (the part that was touching the animal's body). Regular leather — the kind used in belts, hard-soled shoes, and briefcases — uses that tough outer surface. Suede is different. It is made from the inner side of the skin.

That inner surface is then sanded or buffed, which causes tiny fibers to stand up from the surface. These upright fibers are called the nap. The nap is what gives suede its soft, fuzzy, velvety feel — almost like a dry velvet fabric.
Which animals does it come from?

Suede can come from lamb, calf (young cow), deer, pig, or goat. Lamb suede is the most common and highly regarded — it is exceptionally soft and fine. In general, the younger the animal, the softer and more delicate the suede tends to be.
What it looks and feels like

Suede has a consistently soft, slightly fuzzy surface. It is not shiny like polished leather — it has a matte, almost dusty look. The color appears rich and deep.

Here is a distinctive feature: if you run your finger across suede in one direction, the nap flattens and the surface looks slightly lighter in color. Run your finger back the other way, and the fibers stand back up, making the color look richer and darker. This directional behavior of the nap is one of suede's most recognizable characteristics.
How suede differs from regular leather

—Regular leather (full-grain)Suede

Regular leather uses the outer side of the skin. That outer layer is dense, tough, naturally smooth, and quite resistant to water and scratches. It's the stronger of the two.

Suede, using the inner side, is:

  • Significantly softer and more flexible
  • Lighter in weight
  • Velvety in texture rather than smooth
  • More delicate and easier to damage
  • Much more vulnerable to water and stains

Think of it this way: regular leather is like a hard shell; suede is the soft lining inside.
Suede vs. Nubuck — an important distinction

This confuses a lot of people. Nubuck also has a soft, fuzzy nap — but it is buffed from the outer side of the hide (usually calfskin). Because the outer side is naturally tougher and more tightly structured, nubuck is slightly more durable and firmer than suede, even though both feel soft and look similar at first glance.

Simple rule to remember: Suede = inner side of skin = softer and more delicate. Nubuck = outer side of skin = slightly tougher and more resistant.
What suede is used for

Suede is prized in fashion and design because of its luxurious feel and elegant, understated appearance. Common uses include:

  • Footwear — Suede shoes and boots are extremely popular. The classic desert boot, Chelsea boots, and many casual sneakers are made in suede.
  • Clothing — Suede jackets, coats, skirts, and trousers appear frequently in fashion. A suede jacket has a distinctive soft drape and warmth.
  • Bags and accessories — Purses, wallets, and gloves made from suede have a premium, soft-to-the-touch feel.
  • Furniture upholstery — Sofas and chairs are sometimes upholstered in suede for a rich, comfortable appearance.
  • Linings and interiors — Because of its softness, suede is often used to line the insides of jewelry boxes, instrument cases, and high-end bags.
Suede's biggest weakness: it's delicate

The inner side of skin is not built to face the world — and that shows. Suede has real vulnerabilities you need to know about.

Water is suede's enemy. Even a light rain can leave visible water marks on suede. Oil and liquid stains are very hard to remove and can permanently discolor the surface. This is why suede products often come with a recommendation to spray them with a waterproofing spray before first use — this creates a protective barrier on the fibers.

Dirt and scuffs are also a problem. The nap traps dust and can flatten in areas that get rubbed often (like the toe of a shoe or the bottom of a bag).

Suede is maintained with a special suede brush — a brush with stiff bristles used to lift the flattened nap back up and to remove dry surface dirt. You should never scrub suede with a wet cloth the way you would clean regular leather or fabric.

For this reason, suede products are generally considered "dry weather" items. Many people avoid wearing suede shoes on rainy days entirely.
Faux suede (synthetic suede)

Because real suede is expensive and requires careful care, many products today use faux suede — also called synthetic suede, microsuede, or vegan suede. This is an artificial material made from very fine polyester or nylon microfibers woven together to mimic the look and feel of real suede. Well-known versions include brands called Ultrasuede and Alcantara (used in luxury car interiors).

Faux suede is:

  • More affordable than real suede
  • Easier to clean
  • More resistant to water and stains
  • Slightly less soft than the finest real suede
  • More uniform in appearance (real suede has natural variation in texture and color)

It is widely used in furniture, car interiors, clothing, and fashion accessories. When a product says "suede" at a low price point, it is often faux suede.
How to tell real suede from faux suede

Real suede has a natural, slightly irregular texture — the fibers are not perfectly uniform. It also breathes (allows air through) and has the natural variation that comes from an animal hide. Faux suede tends to look slightly more uniform and synthetic under close inspection, and it does not breathe as naturally.
The word used in everyday speech

When people say something is "suede" or "in suede," they simply mean it has that soft, velvety, napped surface — whether from real leather or synthetic material. "A pair of suede boots" immediately tells you those boots are soft, matte-textured, and require gentle care. It signals a certain luxurious softness and a slightly fashion-forward or classic aesthetic.
Summary

Suede is leather made from the inner side of animal skin, sanded to produce a soft, fuzzy, velvety surface called the nap. It is softer and more flexible than regular leather, but also more delicate — it marks easily, absorbs water, and needs careful maintenance. It is used in shoes, clothing, bags, and furniture. Synthetic versions (faux suede) replicate its appearance at lower cost and with greater durability. The word "suede" signals softness, a matte velvety texture, and a certain refined quality in any product it describes.
15445:
Sufferance means passive, reluctant tolerance — allowing something to happen or continue not because you approve of it or want it, but simply because you are not actively stopping it.

It describes a specific zone between full approval and outright refusal. Think of it as a spectrum:

  • Active welcome → "You are wanted here."
  • Sufferance → "I'm not throwing you out. But I'm not glad you're here either."
  • Outright refusal → "You are not allowed here at all."

When something exists "at sufferance," it exists not because it has earned its place, but because someone in authority has quietly chosen not to push it away — at least for now.

The phrase you will encounter most often is "on sufferance." It means being tolerated without being truly accepted, valued, or welcomed.

Examples:

  • An employee who is performing badly but hasn't been fired yet is being kept on sufferance. The employer hasn't dismissed them, but they're not valued — they're just still there, for now.
  • Imagine showing up uninvited to a gathering. The host knows you and doesn't ask you to leave, but doesn't greet you warmly either. You are there "on sufferance" — tolerated, not welcomed.
  • A country that allows migrants to stay without granting them any legal status is letting them remain on sufferance.

What "on sufferance" always implies is insecurity. The tolerance could be withdrawn at any moment. You are not there by right — you're there only because someone has decided, for now, to look the other way. The moment they change their mind, your position disappears.

This is what gives the word a slightly undignified, uncomfortable feel: to exist on sufferance is to be dependent on someone else's mercy, not on your own standing or rights.

The word has one very precise and well-known legal use: tenancy at sufferance.

This describes a specific situation:

  • A person had a valid, legal right to occupy a property — say, a renter with a lease.
  • That right has now expired (the lease ended).
  • But the person is still living there.
  • The property owner has not formally asked them to leave — but has not renewed their permission either.

For example: Ravi had a lease on an apartment until June 30th. It is now August, and he is still living there. The landlord has not renewed the lease but has not filed for eviction either. Ravi is now a tenant at sufferance — his legal right to be there has ended, he has no formal new permission to stay, but the landlord is passively allowing it by taking no action.

Tenancy at sufferance is the weakest possible form of occupancy. It is not based on a contract or any agreement. It exists purely because the landlord hasn't moved to end it yet. The moment the landlord acts, it ends.
The Older Meaning: Endurance of Hardship

In older or more formal writing — particularly literature — "sufferance" was also used to mean the patient endurance of pain, difficulty, or mistreatment — the ability to bear hardship quietly.

Example: "She bore the cruelties of her circumstance with silent sufferance."
Here it means she endured the hardships with patience, without complaint or resistance.

You will also encounter the phrase "beyond sufferance" — meaning beyond what any person can be expected to tolerate or endure:

  • "The cruelty was beyond sufferance." → The cruelty was so extreme it could no longer be borne.

This meaning is less common in everyday modern English, but it is worth knowing because you will encounter it in classic literature and formal writing.

1. Passive tolerance / grudging allowance — allowing something to exist or continue without objecting, even though you do not approve. This is the dominant, most important modern meaning.
  2. "On sufferance" — existing or being present only because one is being tolerated, not because one is genuinely welcome or has a rightful place.
  3. Tenancy at sufferance (legal) — occupying property after one's legal right to do so has expired, with neither formal new permission nor formal eviction.
  4. Patient endurance of hardship (older/literary) — quietly bearing pain, indignity, or difficulty without resistance.
The One Thread That Connects All Meanings

Whether you look at the modern meaning, the legal meaning, or the older literary meaning, one idea runs through all of them: things being allowed to continue without active consent or approval.

The landlord isn't stopping the tenant → tenancy at sufferance.
The host isn't throwing the uninvited guest out → the guest is there on sufferance.
The person isn't fighting back against hardship → they're enduring it in sufferance.

In every case, sufferance is about passive allowing, never enthusiastic accepting. And wherever the word appears, it carries a quiet suggestion that the situation is fragile, undignified, and entirely dependent on the continued patience of whoever holds the power to end it.
15446:
Suffering is the experience of going through something deeply painful, difficult, or distressing — and having to endure it. It is what a person (or animal) feels inside when they are in pain, deeply hurt, or burdened by hardship. The key idea is not just the pain itself, but the experience of living through it.

Think of it this way: if you touch a hot stove, you feel pain in an instant. But if you are sick for weeks, lying in bed, unable to eat, feeling miserable day after day — that prolonged, heavy, inward experience of bearing all of that? That is suffering.

Suffering is not just about physical pain. It has three main forms:

1. Physical suffering — pain that comes from the body. Serious illness, injury, starvation, or extreme cold can all cause physical suffering. It is what a cancer patient feels during aggressive treatment, or what a person feels when starving.

2. Emotional suffering — pain that lives in the heart and feelings. Grief after losing someone you love, the anguish of a broken relationship, deep loneliness, shame, fear, or despair — all of these are forms of suffering. A person can be physically healthy and still suffer enormously.

3. Mental suffering — pain that lives in the mind. Anxiety that never lets you rest, the torment of guilt, the helplessness of watching your life fall apart — these cause real, serious suffering even without a single physical wound.

It is common for all three to combine. A seriously ill person may suffer physically from their disease, emotionally from fear of death, and mentally from the feeling of losing control over their life.

To truly understand the word, you need to understand what makes suffering suffering and not just "a bad moment."

  • It is inward and subjective. Suffering is felt inside a person. Two people can go through the same event — say, losing a job — and one might suffer deeply while the other takes it in stride. The external event is the same; the suffering depends on the person experiencing it.
  • It has duration. Suffering is not just a flash of pain. It is something you go through and bear over time. Even brief suffering has the quality of feeling like a burden you are carrying, not just a sensation that passed.
  • It implies endurance. This is subtle but important. The word "suffering" carries the idea of continuing to exist through something painful. You do not just feel it once and move on — you are in a state of it. This is why we say someone is "suffering from" a disease, not simply "feeling" it.
  • It is unwanted. Suffering is never chosen. It is imposed — by life, by circumstance, by other people, by the body, by the mind. This is what separates it from, say, the discomfort of exercise, which you choose and which has an enjoyable goal.

Suffering exists on a scale. Not all suffering is equal.

  • At the mild end: persistent unhappiness, worry, discomfort that weighs on you.
  • In the middle: deep sadness, grief, significant distress, misery.
  • At the severe end: anguish, agony, torment — suffering so intense it consumes a person entirely and can feel unbearable.

The word "suffering" covers this whole range, though it leans toward the serious and significant. We generally do not say someone is "suffering" because they stubbed a toe. We use it when the pain or hardship is meaningful in scale or duration.

These words are close in meaning but are not identical:

Pain is more specific — it usually refers to the raw, immediate sensation (most often physical). Suffering is broader. It includes pain, but it also includes the burden of living through it, and it extends into emotional and mental territory that the word "pain" does not always reach.

Misery is suffering combined with a sense of wretchedness and hopelessness — a state of being deeply unhappy and poor in spirit.

Agony is extreme, intense suffering — the sharpest end of the scale. All agony is suffering, but not all suffering is agony.

Anguish is intense emotional or mental suffering specifically — the kind that twists and torments from the inside. A parent waiting to hear if their child survived an accident is in anguish.

Distress is suffering with a sense of urgency and being overwhelmed — it often implies that something is happening right now that is too much to handle.

Suffering (as a noun) is used in several natural ways:

  • To describe a state someone is in:
    "She has endured years of suffering."
  • To describe the suffering caused by something:
    "The war brought immense suffering to the civilian population."
  • To describe the goal of reducing it:
    "The doctor's duty is to relieve the patient's suffering."
  • To describe its type or origin:
    "He struggled with emotional suffering long after the accident."

Common words that naturally pair with "suffering":

  • Verbs: cause, inflict, relieve, alleviate, ease, endure, witness, reduce, avoid.
  • Adjectives: great, immense, unnecessary, needless, human, silent, prolonged, intense.
  • Phrases: "human suffering," "unnecessary suffering," "relieve suffering," "a source of suffering."

Suffering is one of the most universal features of conscious life. Every human being — and many animals — experiences it. It is precisely because suffering is so fundamental that it sits at the centre of ethics (causing unnecessary suffering is considered wrong), medicine (the purpose of healing is partly to reduce suffering), and philosophy and religion (many of the world's great traditions — Buddhism, Christianity, Stoicism — have developed entire frameworks for understanding and responding to suffering).

When you encounter the word "suffering," the question to always ask is: who is experiencing it, what is causing it, how intense is it, and how long has it gone on? The answer to those questions tells you everything about the specific suffering being described.
15447:
To suffice means to be enough for a particular purpose or need. That is the heart of it. When something suffices, it meets the requirement — it does the job, it covers the need, it is adequate.

Think of it as a simple test: does X meet the minimum requirement? If yes, X suffices.
The Key Nuance: "Enough" — Not More, Not Less

This is critical to understand. "Suffice" sits right at the line of adequacy. It does not mean excellent, outstanding, or more than enough. It means at least enough — it clears the bar.

A single candle may suffice to light a small room. (It gives enough light — not great, but it works.) One explanation may suffice. (You do not need another — this one is adequate.) So when something suffices, you can stop searching. The need is met.

This verb works in three main patterns:

Pattern 1 — [Something] suffices:
The subject is simply "enough" on its own.

  • "This amount will suffice."
  • "A brief explanation suffices here."
  • "One copy suffices."

Pattern 2 — [Something] suffices for [a purpose or person]:
You name what it is enough for.

  • "This food will suffice for the whole group."
  • "A simple apology will not suffice for the damage caused."
  • "Two hours sufficed for the task."

Pattern 3 — [Something] suffices to [do something]:
You name what goal is accomplished.

  • "One dose suffices to relieve the pain."
  • "A few sentences sufficed to explain the problem."
The Most Common Phrase: "Suffice It to Say"

You will encounter this phrase very frequently. It means: "It is enough to say..." or "Let me just say this much..."

You use it when you do not want to go into full detail, but you want to make one key point clearly — usually because the full story would be too long, too painful, or simply unnecessary.

  • "Suffice it to say, the meeting did not go well." (= I won't give you every detail, but know this: it was bad.)
  • "I won't describe the whole ordeal — suffice it to say, it was the worst night of my life."
  • "He lied, he cheated, and — suffice it to say — we are no longer friends."

Think of this phrase as a way of saying: "This one statement captures everything you need to know."

"Suffice" is somewhat formal. In casual, everyday spoken English, people usually say "be enough" or "do" instead:

  • Casual: "Will this be enough?" / "This will do."
  • Formal: "Will this suffice?" / "This will suffice."

Both mean exactly the same thing. But "suffice" sounds more polished and considered, and is especially common in writing, professional settings, academic contexts, and careful speech.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what "suffice" does not mean:

It does not mean excellent. If something suffices, it is adequate — not necessarily great. "The meal sufficed" tells you people were fed. It says nothing about whether the food was delicious.

It does not mean emotionally satisfy. "That answer satisfied me" suggests you were pleased, even moved. "That answer sufficed" simply means it was enough — it answered the question. The emotional weight is absent.

It does not mean prove. You can say "this evidence suffices" (= there is enough of it), but the word itself is only saying the quantity or quality meets a threshold — not that a conclusion has been proven.

This is equally important, and very commonly used. When something does not suffice, it falls short — it is not enough.

  • "I'm afraid a verbal promise will not suffice. We need it in writing."
  • "Good intentions do not suffice — results matter."
  • "One day of practice will not suffice to master this skill."

The negative form often carries a tone of firm, clear rejection. The speaker is saying that whatever has been offered or done simply does not clear the bar.

In everyday life:

  • "Is there enough rice?" / "Yes, this should suffice for dinner."
  • "I only have five minutes — will that suffice to explain the issue?"

In professional or formal settings:

  • "A one-page summary will suffice; there is no need for a full report."
  • "Your signature on this form will suffice."
  • "The committee decided the available evidence did not suffice to reach a verdict."

In writing and literature:

  • "A single glance sufficed to tell her everything."
  • "No words could suffice to express his gratitude."
One Final Way to Think About It

Imagine a cup. Your need is the cup. Something suffices when it fills that cup — right to the brim, or at least enough to serve its purpose. It does not overflow (that would be more than enough). It does not leave the cup half-empty (that would not suffice). It simply meets the level.

That is "suffice" in its entirety: to meet the level of what is needed — no more is required, and no less will do.
15448:
Sufficiency means the state of having enough — enough of something to meet a need, fulfill a purpose, or satisfy a requirement.

It describes a condition where the amount or quality of something is adequate — not falling short, and not necessarily more than what is needed.

Think of it as sitting at the threshold: on one side is too little, on the other side is more than enough, and sufficiency is right at the point where a need is met.

Sufficiency is almost always measured relative to something — a purpose, a need, a task, or a standard. This is crucial.

You cannot just say "there is sufficiency" in a vacuum and have it mean much. You usually ask: sufficient for what?

  • A cup of water might be sufficiency for washing your hands, but not for filling a tank.
  • One lamp might be sufficiency for reading in a room, but not for lighting a stadium.
  • A thousand rupees might be sufficiency for a week's groceries, but not for buying a car.

So sufficiency is always contextual — it depends entirely on the need being measured against.

This is where many learners go wrong, so pay close attention.

Sufficiency ≠ Abundance or Plenty
Abundance means more than enough — a generous surplus. Sufficiency makes no such claim. It simply says the bar has been cleared.

Sufficiency ≠ Excess or Surplus
Excess means you have gone past what is needed. Sufficiency sits right at or just past the threshold — it does not carry the idea of overflow or waste.

Sufficiency ≠ Scarcity or Shortage
These are the opposites. Scarcity means there is not enough. Sufficiency is the negation of scarcity.

ConceptRelationship to need
ScarcityBelow the threshold — not enough
SufficiencyAt or just past the threshold — enough
AbundanceWell above the threshold — more than enough

Sufficiency is a formal word. You are unlikely to hear it in casual conversation. In spoken English, people say "enough" instead.

  • Casual: "We have enough rice."
  • Formal: "There is a sufficiency of rice."

You will encounter "sufficiency" more often in:

  • Academic writing
  • Philosophy and ethics
  • Economics and policy discussions
  • Legal and formal documents
  • Literature (especially older texts)
How It Is Used in Sentences

As a standalone noun:

"The report questioned the sufficiency of the evidence presented in court."

(= whether the evidence was adequate/enough to support the conclusion)

"The minister expressed doubt about the sufficiency of the aid package."

(= whether the aid package was large enough to meet the need)

In the construction "a sufficiency of":
This is a classic, slightly old-fashioned phrase, but you will still see it in literature and formal writing.

"He had earned a sufficiency of money to retire comfortably."

(= enough money, adequate money)

"The committee was satisfied that there was a sufficiency of data to proceed."

When something fails to reach sufficiency:

"Critics argued the new law lacked sufficiency in addressing climate change."

(= it did not go far enough)

In philosophy and ethics, sufficiency has a deeper, more specific meaning — and it is worth knowing this because it shows up in serious writing and debate.

There is a principle called the sufficiency principle (associated with the philosopher Harry Frankfurt), which argues that what matters morally is not that everyone has equal amounts, but that everyone has enough. The focus shifts from equality to a threshold.

For example:

  • An equality argument says: Everyone should have the same income.
  • A sufficiency argument says: Everyone should have enough income to live a dignified life — whether that is exactly equal or not is secondary.

This is why you often see "sufficiency" in debates about poverty, welfare, justice, and distribution of resources. The question becomes: has this person or group reached sufficiency? — meaning, do they have enough to meet their basic needs and live a reasonable life?

This concept is also the basis of sufficiency economics, a development philosophy (famously promoted in Thailand) that encourages people and communities to produce and consume enough — avoiding excess and protecting against risk — rather than constantly chasing growth and surplus.

You will also encounter the phrase sufficient condition in logic, mathematics, and philosophy. While this involves the adjective form, understanding it will help you see how the noun "sufficiency" operates in that world.

A sufficient condition for something means: if this condition is true, then the result is guaranteed.

For example:

  • Being a square is a sufficient condition for being a rectangle. (All squares are rectangles — if something is a square, that alone guarantees it is a rectangle.)
  • It is NOT a necessary condition, because rectangles exist that are not squares.

Sufficiency, in this context, refers to the quality of being enough — by itself — to guarantee an outcome.

"The court must evaluate the sufficiency of each condition independently."

This is different from necessity. Something can be sufficient without being necessary, and necessary without being sufficient.

The compound self-sufficiency is very commonly used and means the ability to provide everything one needs for oneself, without depending on external sources.

  • A self-sufficient farm grows all its own food.
  • A self-sufficient nation does not rely on imports for its basic needs.
  • A self-sufficient person can manage without help from others.

The "self-" prefix just specifies the source from which sufficiency is achieved — from within, rather than from outside.

Knowing the related forms helps you use the word correctly in writing:

  • Sufficient (adjective): The evidence was sufficient to convict.
  • Sufficiently (adverb): She was not sufficiently prepared for the exam.
  • Sufficiency (noun): There was no sufficiency of proof.
  • Insufficient (adjective — opposite): The funding was insufficient.
  • Insufficiency (noun — opposite): An insufficiency of sleep leads to poor concentration.
  • Self-sufficient (adjective): The village became self-sufficient in food.
  • Self-sufficiency (noun): They valued self-sufficiency above all.

Sufficiency is the condition of having exactly enough of something to meet a need or fulfill a purpose — sitting at the threshold between shortage and surplus, always measured against a specific requirement or standard.
15449:
Sufficient means enough to meet a need or purpose — not too little, and not necessarily more than needed. Just the right amount to satisfy a requirement.

Think of it like filling a bucket that needs to be full to water a garden. If you pour in exactly enough water to fill it, that water is sufficient. If you pour in less, it's not sufficient. If you pour in extra, well, that's more than sufficient — but the point is, sufficient simply means the need is met.
The Key Insight: Sufficient Is Always Relative to a Goal

This is the most important thing to understand: sufficient never stands alone in meaning. It always answers the question, "Enough for what?"

The same amount can be sufficient in one situation and completely insufficient in another.

  • One candle may be sufficient to light a small room, but not sufficient to light a stadium.
  • Three hours of sleep might be sufficient for a short nap, but not sufficient for a full night's rest.
  • A pinch of salt may be sufficient for a single egg, but not sufficient for a large pot of pasta.

The word is always pointing at a specific standard or purpose. Once that purpose is met, the thing qualifies as sufficient.

Understanding a word also means knowing what it doesn't mean.

Sufficient ≠ Plentiful or Abundant
Sufficient doesn't suggest that there's a lot of something. It only says there's enough. If you have just barely enough money to pay a bill, that money is sufficient — even if it leaves you with nothing left over.

Sufficient ≠ Perfect or Ideal
Something can be sufficient without being great or ideal. A simple meal can be sufficient to keep you from being hungry. It doesn't have to be a feast.

Sufficient ≠ More Than Enough
Words like ample, abundant, or plentiful go further — they mean more than what's needed. Sufficient stays right at the line of "just enough."

The direct opposite of sufficient is insufficient, which means not enough — falling short of what is needed.

  • There was insufficient evidence to prove he was guilty. (Not enough evidence.)
  • She had insufficient time to finish the exam. (Not enough time.)

"Sufficient" is slightly more formal than its close cousin "enough." In everyday speech, people usually say enough. In writing, legal language, academic work, science, and professional settings, sufficient is very common.

Casual: "Do we have enough food for the party?"
Formal: "The provisions should be sufficient for all attendees."

Both sentences mean the same thing. The difference is just the level of formality.
How It Behaves in a Sentence

As an adjective, "sufficient" usually appears in two positions:

Before a noun:

  • "We need sufficient time to complete the project."
  • "She gave sufficient reasons for her decision."

After a linking verb (like "is," "was," "seems"):

  • "The evidence is sufficient."
  • "One coat of paint was sufficient."
  • "Your explanation seems sufficient."

It is also commonly followed by "to + verb" or "for + noun" to name the purpose:

  • "Is this rope strong enough?" → "Is this rope sufficient to hold the weight?"
  • "There is sufficient funding for the research."
  • "She had sufficient skill to pass the test."

Law:
"The prosecution did not present sufficient evidence to secure a conviction."
→ The evidence didn't meet the legal standard required. Not enough.

Science:
"The temperature was sufficient to cause the chemical reaction."
→ The temperature reached the threshold needed to trigger the reaction.

Daily Life:
"I don't think I have sufficient cash on me — can I pay by card?"
→ The speaker's cash might not cover the cost.

Work:
"Your qualifications are sufficient for this role."
→ You meet the requirements. You qualify.

Instructions:
"Add water until the mixture is of sufficient consistency."
→ Keep adding water until the mixture reaches the right thickness.

In logic and reasoning, you'll often see the phrase "sufficient condition." This means: if this thing is true or present, it guarantees a result.

For example: "Being over 18 is a sufficient condition to vote in many countries." If you're over 18, that alone is enough — you qualify. You don't need anything else on top of that.

This is a precise, logical use of the word and you'll see it often in academic or analytical writing.

Sufficient = Enough to meet a specific need or purpose — no more is required, and nothing is lacking.

It's a word about meeting a threshold. It's context-sensitive, slightly formal, and always implies a standard being measured against. When something is sufficient, the job is done — the requirement is satisfied.
